code.title: List vs tuple: mutability, hashing, shallow immutability
code.python:
# A list can change; a tuple cannot, so only the tuple can be a dict key.
lst = [1, 2]
tup = (1, 2)
lst.append(3)                      # fine: lists are mutable
print("list after append:", lst)
try:
    tup.append(3)                  # tuples have no append
except AttributeError as e:
    print("tuple error:", e)

grid = {(0, 0): "start", (2, 3): "goal"}   # tuple keys are hashable
print("lookup (2, 3):", grid[(2, 3)])
try:
    {[0, 0]: "x"}                  # list keys are not allowed
except TypeError as e:
    print("list key error:", e)

# Immutability is shallow: the tuple holds a list, and the list can change.
t = ([1], 2)
t[0].append(99)
print("tuple with mutated inner list:", t)
try:
    hash(t)
except TypeError as e:
    print("hash error:", e)

followUps:
A dict key must have a hash that never changes while it sits in the table, and a tuple of hashable items satisfies that because its contents cannot change. A list can change, so its content-based hash would change too, and the dict would look in the wrong slot and lose the entry. So Python refuses: list.__hash__ is None.

Example: (2, 3) always hashes the same, so d[(2, 3)] finds the same slot every time. Lookup stays O(1) on average.

It raises a TypeError, but the list still gets changed first. The line t[0] += [3] first runs t[0].__iadd__([3]), which extends the inner list in place (it becomes [1, 3]), and then tries to store the result back into t[0], which a tuple forbids.

t = ([1], 2)
try: t[0] += [3]
except TypeError: pass
print(t)   # ([1, 3], 2)

The lesson: tuple immutability is shallow, and the error arrives after the mutation.

code.title: Falsy values and what or/and really return
code.python:
# Show which values are falsy, and that or/and return operands, not bools.
values = [0, 0.0, "", [], (), {}, set(), None, False, "0", [0], -1]
for v in values:
    print(repr(v).ljust(6), "->", bool(v))

print("'' or 'Guest'   ->", repr("" or "Guest"))
print("'Ann' or 'Guest'->", repr("Ann" or "Guest"))
print("0 or 'default'  ->", repr(0 or "default"))     # 0 is valid but replaced!
print("[] and 5        ->", repr([] and 5))            # first falsy operand
print("3 and 5         ->", repr(3 and 5))             # last operand
print("0 and 1/0       ->", repr(0 and 1 / 0))         # right side never runs

count = 0
print("safe default    ->", count if count is not None else 10)

class Box:
    def __len__(self):             # truthiness falls back to __len__
        return 0
print("empty Box       ->", bool(Box()))

followUps:
It evaluates to 0, and no error happens. and stops at the first falsy operand and returns it, so the right side 1/0 is never evaluated. This is called short-circuiting.

The opposite case: 1 and 1/0 does raise ZeroDivisionError, because the left side is truthy and Python must look at the right. The same idea with or: 5 or 1/0 returns 5 safely. Short-circuiting is why if x and x.ok: is a safe guard.

Because truth is ambiguous for an array: the question "is this array true?" could mean any element, all elements, or non-empty, and NumPy refuses to guess. It raises ValueError: The truth value of an array with more than one element is ambiguous.

Be explicit instead: arr.any(), arr.all(), or arr.size > 0. A one-element array does have a clear truth value (np.array([0]) is falsy), which is why this bug can hide until the data grows.

code.title: Mutable default argument bug and the None-sentinel fix
code.python:
# Default values are created once, when "def" runs, not on every call.
def add_bad(x, acc=[]):
    acc.append(x)
    return acc

print("bad  :", add_bad(1), add_bad(2), add_bad(3))
print("stored default:", add_bad.__defaults__)

def add_good(x, acc=None):
    if acc is None:               # sentinel: build a fresh list per call
        acc = []
    acc.append(x)
    return acc

print("good :", add_good(1), add_good(2), add_good(3))

# Passing your own list always works, in both versions.
mine = []
add_bad(7, mine)
print("own list:", mine)

# The shared default can be a deliberate cache, but it is easy to misread.
def fib(n, memo={0: 0, 1: 1}):
    if n not in memo:
        memo[n] = fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2)
    return memo[n]
print("fib(30) =", fib(30))

followUps:
Because if not acc is true for any empty container, including an empty list the caller passed on purpose. Then your code throws away the caller's list and builds a new one, so their list never receives the appended items.

def add(x, acc=None):
    if not acc: acc = []   # bug
    acc.append(x)
mine = []
add(1, mine)   # mine is still []

With is None, the empty list mine is kept, and the append is visible to the caller.

Yes, the same rule applies: datetime.now() runs once, when the def executes, so every call that omits the argument gets the same frozen timestamp from when the module loaded. It is not a mutation problem, but it is the same evaluate-once cause.

def log(msg, stamp=None):
    if stamp is None:
        stamp = datetime.now()

Use the None sentinel for anything that must be fresh per call: lists, dicts, times, random values.

code.title: Pass by object reference: mutate vs rebind
code.python:
# The parameter is another name for the caller's object.
def mutate(lst):
    lst.append(99)                # changes the shared object
def rebind(lst):
    lst = [0]                     # only the local name moves
    return lst
def add_one(n):
    n += 1                        # ints are immutable: new object, local name
    return n

a = [1, 2]
mutate(a)
print("after mutate:", a)
rebind(a)
print("after rebind:", a, "(unchanged)")

n = 5
add_one(n)
print("int after add_one:", n)

def show_ids(lst):
    print("inside id same as caller:", id(lst) == id(a))
show_ids(a)

def clear_in_place(lst):
    lst.clear()                   # mutate, do not rebind
clear_in_place(a)
print("after clear_in_place:", a)

def safe_sorted(lst):
    return sorted(lst)            # returns a new list, caller's is untouched
b = [3, 1, 2]
print("safe_sorted:", safe_sorted(b), "original:", b)

followUps:
Mutate the object itself instead of rebinding the name: call lst.clear(), or use slice assignment lst[:] = []. Both keep the same list object, so the caller sees it empty. Writing lst = [] would only repoint the local name.

def clear_in_place(lst):
    lst.clear()
nums = [1, 2, 3]
clear_in_place(nums)   # nums == []

Cost is O(n) to release the references and O(1) extra space.

Work on a copy, or return a new object instead of changing the argument. Copy at the top with items = list(items) (shallow) or copy.deepcopy(items) if nested objects might change. Prefer non-mutating tools such as sorted(x) over x.sort(), and return the result.

Other safeguards: accept tuples or other immutable types, name in-place functions clearly (sort_in_place), and document it. A shallow copy still shares inner lists, so [[1],[2]] needs deepcopy.

code.title: A for loop is iter() plus next() until StopIteration
code.python:
# for x in obj  is the same as the manual loop below.
nums = [10, 20, 30]

print("for loop:")
for x in nums:
    print("  ", x)

print("manual loop:")
it = iter(nums)                   # step 1: ask for an iterator
while True:
    try:
        x = next(it)              # step 2: pull one item at a time
    except StopIteration:         # step 3: this ends the loop quietly
        break
    print("  ", x)

# Iterators are single-use: they are used up after one pass.
pairs = zip("ab", [1, 2])
print("first pass :", list(pairs))
print("second pass:", list(pairs))

# A custom iterable: any class with __iter__ and __next__ works in for.
class Countdown:
    def __init__(self, n): self.n = n
    def __iter__(self): return self
    def __next__(self):
        if self.n == 0:
            raise StopIteration
        self.n -= 1
        return self.n + 1
print("countdown:", list(Countdown(3)))

followUps:
Here is the equivalent loop, written by hand:

it = iter(obj)
while True:
    try: x = next(it)
    except StopIteration: break
    body(x)

The loop-else would run where the except branch ends the loop, and only if no break fired from the body. For a list of 3 items, next is called 4 times: three values, then StopIteration.

Because a zip object is its own iterator, and an iterator is consumed as you read it. After the first pass it is exhausted, so iter(z) returns the same finished object and next raises StopIteration immediately.

Example: z = zip('ab', [1, 2]); list(z) gives [('a', 1), ('b', 2)], and a second list(z) gives []. A list is different: it is an iterable that hands out a fresh iterator each time. Store list(z) if you need to reuse the pairs.

code.title: for/else runs only when there was no break

followUps:
Yes. The else runs whenever the loop finishes without break, and a loop that never executes its body has trivially not broken. So for x in []: ... else: print('done') prints done.

This matters in searches: with an empty list, the not-found branch correctly runs. It also means else is not "if the loop ran"; it is "if the loop did not break".

Use any() (or next() with a default) and drop the flag and the else:

def is_prime(n):
    return n > 1 and not any(
        n % d == 0 for d in range(2, isqrt(n) + 1))

It short-circuits at the first divisor just like break, so the cost is the same, O(sqrt n) time and O(1) space. To get the found item itself, use next((d for d in ds if ok(d)), None).

code.title: Dict hashing: O(1) lookup, collisions and insertion order

followUps:
The entry is effectively lost. The dict stored the key in the slot for its old hash, so a lookup with the new hash probes a different slot and does not find it, even though the object is still in the table. That is why keys must be immutable or at least keep a stable hash.

Example: if a class hashes on a field and you change the field after inserting, obj in d returns False while len(d) still counts it.

For security: with a fixed hash function, an attacker could send many keys that collide and turn every dict operation into O(n), slowing a server to a crawl (a hash-flooding denial of service). Python seeds string and bytes hashing with a random value at startup, so collisions cannot be planned in advance.

The side effect is that hash('abc') differs between runs, so never persist hashes or rely on set order of strings. Set PYTHONHASHSEED to make it repeatable for tests.

code.title: Why a list cannot be a dict key; tuple and frozenset can
code.python:
# A hash must not change while the key is stored.
for name, obj in [("tuple", (1, 2)), ("frozenset", frozenset([1, 2])),
                  ("str", "ab"), ("list", [1, 2]), ("set", {1, 2}),
                  ("dict", {1: 2}), ("tuple with list", (1, [2]))]:
    try:
        print(name.ljust(16), "hash ok:", isinstance(hash(obj), int))
    except TypeError as e:
        print(name.ljust(16), "error:", e)

# Convert unhashable data to something hashable to use it as a key.
seen = {}
for row in [[1, 2], [3, 4], [1, 2]]:
    key = tuple(row)              # list -> tuple
    seen[key] = seen.get(key, 0) + 1
print("counts:", seen)

# Unordered content: frozenset ignores order.
print("frozenset equal:", frozenset([1, 2]) == frozenset([2, 1]))
print("same hash      :", hash(frozenset([1, 2])) == hash(frozenset([2, 1])))

# Equal objects must have equal hashes.
print("1 == 1.0:", 1 == 1.0, " same hash:", hash(1) == hash(1.0))

followUps:
No. A tuple is hashable only if every item in it is hashable, because its hash is built from its items' hashes. (1, [2]) contains a list, so hash((1, [2])) raises TypeError: unhashable type: 'list'.

Compare (1, (2, 3)) and (1, 'a'), which are fine. Note the tuple itself is immutable, but its inner list can still be changed, which is exactly why Python refuses to hash it.

By identity. A plain class gets __hash__ from object, based on its memory address (id), and __eq__ defaults to identity too. So two separate instances are never equal, even with the same field values, and each acts as its own key.

If you define __eq__ and not __hash__, Python sets __hash__ to None and the class becomes unhashable. To use value-based keys, define both from the same immutable fields, e.g. hash((self.x, self.y)), or use @dataclass(frozen=True).

code.title: Slicing rules, copy cost, and negative steps
code.python:
a = [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
print("a[1:4]   ", a[1:4])         # start included, stop excluded
print("a[-2:]   ", a[-2:])         # negative index counts from the end
print("a[::2]   ", a[::2])         # step 2
print("a[::-1]  ", a[::-1])        # reversed copy
print("a[4:1:-1]", a[4:1:-1])      # negative step: start must be larger
print("a[10:20] ", a[10:20])       # out of range is clamped, no error
print("a[-0:]   ", a[-0:])         # -0 is 0, so the whole list

# A slice copies references: changing the copy leaves the original alone.
b = a[1:4]
b[0] = 99
print("copy changed:", b, " original:", a)

# Recursion with slices copies O(n) each level: total O(n^2).
def total_slow(xs):
    return 0 if not xs else xs[0] + total_slow(xs[1:])   # copies every call
def total_fast(xs, i=0):
    return 0 if i == len(xs) else xs[i] + total_fast(xs, i + 1)   # no copy
print("sums:", total_slow(list(range(100))), total_fast(list(range(100))))

# Lazy slicing of any iterator with itertools.
from itertools import islice
print("islice:", list(islice(iter(range(100)), 3, 8, 2)))

followUps:
It returns the whole list. In Python -0 is just 0, so a[-0:] is a[0:], a full copy. People expect "the last zero items", which is a classic trap.

For a = [1, 2, 3]: a[-0:] is [1, 2, 3], but a[len(a)-0:] is []. If a count k may be zero, write a[len(a)-k:] instead of a[-k:].

Use itertools.islice(it, start, stop, step). It walks the iterator and yields only the wanted items, without building a list, and it works on generators and files where [ ] slicing is not allowed.

from itertools import islice
first5 = list(islice(gen, 5))
evens = islice(gen, 0, None, 2)

It cannot jump: skipping to start costs O(start) because it must consume those items, and negative indexes are not supported.

code.title: is compares identity, == compares value
code.python:
a = [1, 2]
b = [1, 2]
c = a
print("a == b:", a == b)          # same value
print("a is b:", a is b)          # different objects
print("a is c:", a is c)          # same object
print("ids differ:", id(a) != id(b))

# Big ints: built at run time, so they are separate objects.
x = int("1000")
y = int("1000")
print("1000 == 1000:", x == y, " is:", x is y)
p = int("100")
q = int("100")
print("100 == 100  :", p == q, " is:", p is q, "(small int cache -5..256)")

# Correct uses of is: singletons such as None.
value = None
print("value is None:", value is None)

# A class can make == lie; is cannot be overridden.
class AlwaysEqual:
    def __eq__(self, other):
        return True
print("AlwaysEqual() == None:", AlwaysEqual() == None)   # noqa
print("AlwaysEqual() is None:", AlwaysEqual() is None)

followUps:
Because == calls __eq__, which a class can override to return anything, so x == None may be True for an object that is not None. x is None checks identity, which cannot be overridden, and there is only one None object. It is also slightly faster, and PEP 8 recommends it.

Real case: NumPy arrays and pandas objects compare elementwise, so arr == None returns an array of results, not one bool.

It is the object's memory address in CPython, a number that is unique among objects that are alive at the same time. a is b is the same as id(a) == id(b).

Do not treat it as permanent: once an object is freed, a new object may reuse the same id. It is also only an address in CPython; other implementations (PyPy) give another kind of unique number. Use it for debugging, not as a key that must stay valid.

code.title: Tuple swap and the order of multiple assignment
code.python:
a, b = 1, 2
a, b = b, a                       # right side becomes (2, 1) first
print("swapped:", a, b)

# Targets are assigned left to right, so a later target may see an earlier one.
nums = [0, 0, 0]
i = 0
i, nums[i] = 1, 9                 # i is rebound first, so nums[1] gets 9
print("i =", i, " nums =", nums)

class Node:
    def __init__(self, v, nxt=None):
        self.v, self.next = v, nxt
def to_list(n):
    out = []
    while n:
        out.append(n.v)
        n = n.next
    return out

# Reverse a linked list 1 -> 2 -> 3 with the safe target order.
head = Node(1, Node(2, Node(3)))
prev, cur = None, head
while cur:
    cur.next, prev, cur = prev, cur, cur.next   # cur.next is assigned first
print("reversed:", to_list(prev))

# Fibonacci in O(1) memory.
x, y = 0, 1
for _ in range(10):
    x, y = y, x + y
print("fib(10) =", x)

followUps:
Keep two numbers and slide them forward with one assignment, so only two values live in memory.

a, b = 0, 1
for _ in range(n):
    a, b = b, a + b
return a

The right side (b, a + b) is built from the old values before either name changes. For n = 10 the pairs go (0,1), (1,1), (1,2), (2,3), ... and a ends at 55. Time is O(n), space is O(1) (the numbers themselves grow, so big n costs more per add).

It builds no tuple. For two names, CPython loads both values onto the stack and uses a ROT_TWO (a SWAP in 3.11+) instruction to exchange them, then stores them: roughly LOAD b, LOAD a, SWAP, STORE a, STORE b. So the swap is as fast as a temporary variable, or faster.

You can check this with import dis; dis.dis('a, b = b, a'). With three names it also avoids a tuple; for four or more it does build one.

code.title: append vs extend, and list.pop(0) vs deque.popleft()
code.python:
import time
from collections import deque

a = [1, 2]
a.append([3, 4])                  # one item: the whole list
b = [1, 2]
b.extend([3, 4])                  # each item added
print("append:", a)
print("extend:", b)

def drain_list(n):
    q = list(range(n))
    while q:
        q.pop(0)                  # shifts every remaining item: O(n)

def drain_deque(n):
    q = deque(range(n))
    while q:
        q.popleft()               # O(1)

for n in (20000, 40000):          # doubling n should ~4x the list time
    t0 = time.perf_counter(); drain_list(n); tl = time.perf_counter() - t0
    t0 = time.perf_counter(); drain_deque(n); td = time.perf_counter() - t0
    print("n =", n, "list slower than deque:", tl > td)

q = deque([1, 2, 3])
q.appendleft(0)
print("deque after appendleft:", list(q), " popleft:", q.popleft())

followUps:
Because a list keeps spare room at the end and only sometimes has to grow. Most appends just write into spare space (cheap). When it is full, Python allocates a bigger array (about 1.125x plus a little) and copies everything, which costs O(n) once.

Since each big copy buys many cheap appends, the total for n appends is O(n), so the average per append is O(1). Example: growing from 0 to 1000 items triggers only a few dozen resizes. A single append can still be slow, hence "amortised".

When the list stays small or you only remove a few items from the front. Shifting 20 pointers takes nanoseconds, and a list has better memory locality and supports indexing in O(1), which a deque does not do in the middle.

Also fine: using a list as a stack (append and pop() at the end), or reading it with an index pointer (i += 1) instead of removing. Switch to deque once the queue can reach thousands of items.

code.title: Positional-only, keyword-only, *args and **kwargs

followUps:
It raises TypeError: f() missing 1 required positional argument: 'a'. Positional-only parameters cannot be given by name, so {'a': 1} is passed as a keyword and no value fills a.

The exception: if the function has **kwargs, the name a goes into kwargs instead of clashing, as in def g(a, /, **kw) where g(1, a=2) works. That freedom is a main reason to use /.

Accept *args, **kwargs in the wrapper and pass them straight on with the same stars: return func(*args, **kwargs). The first star unpacks the tuple into positional arguments and the second unpacks the dict into keyword arguments, so the callee sees exactly what the caller sent.

def wrapper(*args, **kwargs):
    return func(*args, **kwargs)

Use functools.wraps(func) to keep the original name and docstring.

code.title: Remove duplicates but keep order
code.python:
items = [3, 1, 3, 2, 1, 5, 2]
print("input:", items)

# 1) dict.fromkeys: keys are unique and keep first-seen order. O(n).
print("fromkeys :", list(dict.fromkeys(items)))

# 2) seen set with an explicit loop. O(n) time, O(n) space.
seen, out = set(), []
for x in items:
    if x not in seen:
        seen.add(x)
        out.append(x)
print("seen set :", out)

# 3) set() removes duplicates but the order is not guaranteed.
print("sorted(set):", sorted(set(items)), "(order is lost)")

# 4) Unhashable items (lists): O(n^2) membership test on the result.
rows = [[1, 2], [3], [1, 2]]
uniq = []
for r in rows:
    if r not in uniq:
        uniq.append(r)
print("lists    :", uniq)

# Keep the LAST occurrence: process the reversed list, then reverse back.
print("keep last:", list(dict.fromkeys(reversed(items)))[::-1])

# In place on a sorted list with two pointers. O(n) time, O(1) space.
s = [1, 1, 2, 2, 2, 3]
w = 1
for r in range(1, len(s)):
    if s[r] != s[w - 1]:
        s[w] = s[r]
        w += 1
del s[w:]
print("sorted in place:", s)

followUps:
Keep a write index w for the next unique slot and a read index r that scans ahead; copy s[r] to s[w] only when it differs from the last kept value, then trim the tail.

w = 1
for r in range(1, len(s)):
    if s[r] != s[w-1]:
        s[w] = s[r]; w += 1
del s[w:]

For [1,1,2,2,3] this gives [1,2,3]. Time O(n), extra space O(1), because equal values sit next to each other in sorted data.

Reverse the input, dedupe, then reverse the result: list(dict.fromkeys(reversed(items)))[::-1]. Reversing makes the last occurrence come first, so "keep the first" now keeps the last.

For [3,1,3,2,1]: reversed is [1,2,3,1,3], deduped is [1,2,3], and reversed again gives [3,2,1]. Check: the last 3 is at index 2, the last 2 at 3, the last 1 at 4, so that order is right. Time O(n), space O(n).
